Naming what
you're seeing.

The first skill in media literacy isn't a checklist. It's a vocabulary. Once you can name what's in front of you, you can decide what to do with it.

Opening Example
08 / 44
Before we define anything

An example to start with.

A piece of misleading content you've almost certainly already seen. What is it, exactly?
Found in a group chat. Reshared 234,000 times.
Concerned Citizen
posted 4h ago
🚨 BREAKING 🚨
They've been treating the tap water in major cities with something they don't want you to know about. Officials are staying silent. Wake up. Share this before it's taken down. 💧⚠️
↻ 234K shares · 💬 18K replies · ♥ 89K reactions
No source · no specifics · no way to verify
still shared 234,000 times
Three holding questions
Q1
Where did you first see something like this?
Q2
Did you believe it, share it, scroll past it, or argue with it?
Q3
What would you call it, in one word?
Hold your one-word answer. We'll come back to it after the next four slides.
Term 01 of 04
09 / 44
No intent to deceive

Misinformation.

TERM · 01
Mis-
"They believe what they're sharing is true."
False or misleading information shared without intent to deceive.
Most of what you see is this. A friend forwards a screenshot. A relative posts an old photo with a new caption. They are not lying, they are mistaken, and they think they are helping.
Example
0:28 · play
"A friend shares a 'breaking' image from a disaster, the photo turns out to be five years old, from a different country. They genuinely thought it was current."
Intent: NONE Response: gentle correction Don't shame. Don't reshare to dunk on. Quietly correct.
Term 02 of 04
10 / 44
Deliberate

Disinformation.

TERM · 02
Dis-
"They know it's false. They want you to spread it."
False or misleading information shared deliberately, to deceive.
The intent is the entire difference. The content can look identical to misinformation. The person originating it knows it isn't true and is hoping you'll pass it on as if it were.
Example
0:25 · play
"A coordinated network of accounts posts the same fabricated 'leaked document' in the days before an election, the content is identical word-for-word across hundreds of profiles."
Intent: DELIBERATE Response: report & don't share Even sharing it to mock it helps the algorithm.
Term 03 of 04
11 / 44
Not always false

Propaganda.

TERM · 03
Pro-
"True facts can still be used to mislead."
Information, often factually selective or emotionally loaded, used to promote a cause or point of view.
Propaganda is harder to spot than a lie. The trick isn't usually what's said, it's what's left out, what's emphasised, and how it's framed. The facts may check out. The story they add up to may not.
Framing
Which words are used, which images are paired with which facts.
Omission
What's missing, context, opposing views, the full chronology.
Emphasis
Which detail leads, which is buried, which is repeated.
Example
0:30 · play
"A campaign poster citing accurate statistics, but only the ones that flatter one side, paired with imagery designed to provoke fear."
Term 04 of 04
12 / 44
Disguised as journalism

Fake news.

TERM · 04
Fake
"Dressed up to look like a real outlet."
News content fabricated to look like legitimate journalism.
Imposter sites that mimic real outlets, same fonts, similar URLs, plausible bylines. Or social posts laid out to look like screenshotted headlines. The goal is to inherit the trust of journalism without doing any of the work.
Imposter sites
A near-identical clone of a real outlet, one letter different in the URL, identical masthead.
Social fakes
Mock-ups designed to look like a screenshot of a real headline that was never published.
Example
0:28 · play
"A screenshot circulates of a 'BBC News' headline, pixel-perfect typography, plausible date, that the BBC never published."
Summary Card · Photographable

The four at a glance.

Same family. Different intent. Different signals to look for.
01
Mis
Misinformation
False or misleading content shared without intent to deceive. The sharer believes it.
02
Dis
Disinformation
False or misleading content shared deliberately, knowing it's false. The sharer wants spread.
03
Pro
Propaganda
Content used to promote a cause. Not always false, selective, emphasised, emotionally loaded.
04
Fake
Fake news
Content disguised as journalism, imposter sites, mock screenshots, fabricated bylines.
The split that matters most
Mis = mistaken.   Dis = deliberate.   Propaganda = persuasive.   Fake = costumed.
The Human Side
14 / 44

Why it spreads.

It isn't because people are stupid. It's because misleading content is engineered to fit how human attention actually works.
Trigger 01
It hits an emotion, fear, anger, outrage.
Calm, accurate corrections don't go viral. Things that make you feel something do.
Trigger 02
Sharing signals belonging.
Passing it on tells your circle which side you're on. The content matters less than the signal.
Trigger 03
It moves faster than verification.
A correction takes hours. A reshare takes a second. By the time the truth arrives, the lie has been seen ten times.
Trigger 04
Sharing makes you look informed.
People share things that feel true, especially when the share itself flatters them.
And the platforms amplify all of this, by design, because engagement is what they're built to maximise. We'll come back to this in Section Three.
Real Impact · Close to Home
15 / 44
This isn't abstract. The cost is real.

Real impact, close to home.

Three short cases. Each is the shape of a story we've all already seen. The headlines below ran. The outcomes below them happened.
Morning Post · Politics Desk
"Early exit polls reveal landslide, final count expected by midnight"
Posted 14:22 · 2 hours before polls closed
RETRACTED
Election: fabricated results circulate hours before the vote closes.
A coordinated push shifts turnout in marginal constituencies. By the time the platform takes action, the count is over.
Health Update Daily · Wellness
"Common household item shown to neutralise virus, doctors confirm"
Source: forwarded from a private group · No author named
FALSE
Public health: false "cure" goes viral during a real outbreak.
People take a substance they shouldn't. Hospitals admit avoidable cases. The originator never identified.
Local Neighbourhood Watch · Group Post
"Sharing widely: local resident pictured below identified as suspect"
Shared 4,200 times in 6 hours · 312 comments
WRONG PERSON
Community: a rumour targets named individuals, with consequences offline.
A neighbourhood post identifies the wrong person. Threats follow. Damage difficult to undo.
The point Not "social media is bad". The point is that the cost is paid by people, not platforms.

Section Two
17 / 44
02

How media
works.

Where information comes from changes how it reaches you, who paid for it to reach you, and what it's most likely to leave out.
Slides in this section
17 → 20
Three Types
18 / 44

Three types of media.

A quick visual breakdown. Most people use all three on the same day.
TYPE · 01
Traditional
Print · Radio · Broadcast TV
Newspapers, magazines, evening news, talk radio. Edited by a named newsroom. Slow, scheduled, finite. You receive it. You don't shape it.
TYPE · 02
Digital
News sites · Blogs · Podcasts
Online versions of outlets, independent sites, newsletters, podcasts. Editorial still applies but cycles are faster, headlines are A/B tested, comments live underneath. You can search. You can comment.
TYPE · 03
Social
Feeds · Reels · Group chats
Posts from anyone, ordered by an algorithm, optimised for engagement. The line between "audience" and "publisher" disappears. You receive it. You shape it. You are it.
Notice As you move left → right, speed goes up, gatekeeping goes down, and your role shifts from audience to participant.
Three Lenses for Comparing
19 / 44

Three lenses for comparing them.

Use these three questions on any source. They determine how reliable the information that reaches you is likely to be.
01
Production & editorial process.
Who decides what gets published? Is there a named editor, a correction process, a code of standards, or is anyone with an account a publisher?
Ask: "Who would I complain to if this was wrong?"
02
Reach & speed.
How fast can it spread, and to how many people? Print is slow. Broadcast is wide but scheduled. Social is instant and unbounded, and a single post can reach more people than a national newspaper.
Ask: "How much time was there to fact-check this?"
03
Funding & incentives.
Who pays, subscribers, advertisers, a state, an algorithm rewarding engagement? Whoever pays shapes what gets made and how it's framed.
Ask: "Who profits if I share this?"
Comparison · One Story Across Three Formats
20 / 44
Prerecorded comparison

Same story, three formats.

A single news story, say a public protest, shown across all three media types. Notice what changes.
01 · TRADITIONAL
Newspaper
"Thousands gather peacefully; police report no incidents."
700-word article · named reporter · printed next morning · editorial sign-off · corrections column
02 · DIGITAL
News site
"LIVE: Thousands gather, what we know so far (updated 14:22)"
Live blog · updated every few minutes · headline A/B tested · comments below · ads in-stream
03 · SOCIAL
Voice note
Forwarded to family group · 4 min ago
▶
0:24 forwarded many times
0:47 voice note, forwarded onward. No source. Cannot be quoted, fact-checked, or searched. Spreads through trusted contacts, ordered by who sent it last. Context optional.
Same event. Same hour. The version that travels furthest is usually the one with the fewest words and the strongest emotion.
Strengths & Failure Modes
21 / 44

No medium is automatically trustworthy.

Each format has things it does well and predictable ways it fails. The skill is recognising the failure modes of the platforms you use most.
Traditional
Digital
Social
Strengths
Editorial chain · slower pace · named accountability · corrections process
Searchable · linkable · multimedia · live updates · large archives
Speed · reach · direct voice · no gatekeepers · diverse voices on the ground
Typical failures
Slow to react · narrow viewpoint · paywalled · misses local stories · house bias
Clickbait headlines · A/B-tested framing · comment-section drift · paywall vs ad model tension
Algorithmic amplification of outrage · imposters · context collapse · coordinated campaigns
Question to ask
"Whose worldview shaped the editorial line here?"
"Is the headline doing more work than the article?"
"Why is the algorithm showing me this, today?"
Working principle No single source is enough. Cross-check before you trust, especially when the post made you feel something fast.
Section Three
22 / 44
03

How your
feed is built.

You don't see "the internet". You see a custom version of it, chosen for you, optimised for something. Once you can name the mechanism, you can read it.
Slides in this section
22 → 26
Mechanism · 01
23 / 44
Mechanism 01

Algorithms.

The system that decides which content appears in your feed, and in what order. Built to maximise engagement, not accuracy, not importance, not wellbeing.
Inputs
Everything you do: scroll speed, taps, dwell time, who you follow, when you check, what you skipped past.
→
Optimiser
A model trained on one question: "What's most likely to keep this user engaged for the next five minutes?"
→
Your feed
A ranked list of posts, most-engaging first. Not most-true. Not most-useful. Most-engaging.
A useful reframe
An algorithm is not "what's popular today". It's what's most likely to keep you here. That distinction matters.
A useful test
If a post makes you angry on cue, ask: why did the system pick this one for me, right now?
Mechanism · 02
24 / 44
Mechanism 02

Filter bubbles.

The personalised information environment you end up inside. The more you engage with something, the more the system shows you similar content, until that is what the world looks like to you.
YOU
Things you agree with
Similar voices
Familiar framing
More of the same
Opposing views
Unfamiliar voices
Contradicting data
Different framing
your bubble
everything outside it
How it forms
Every "like", every long pause on a video, every click on one side of an argument is a vote for "show me more of that". The system listens.
Why it's a problem
Not because one viewpoint is wrong, but because you stop noticing that another viewpoint exists at all. The disagreement disappears, and so does the practice of weighing it.
A counter-move
Once a week: read one piece on a topic you care about from a source you wouldn't usually read.
Mechanism · 03
25 / 44
Mechanism 03

Echo chambers.

Online communities where similar views are repeated and reinforced, and contrasting views get filtered out, or pushed back against, hard, until they stop turning up.
Inside the chamber
"Exactly this."
"Couldn't agree more."
"This is what I've been saying."
"Spot on."
"Finally someone said it."
"💯💯💯"
"I think there's another side..."
"Preach."
"Have you considered..."
Dissenting voices either get drowned out, ratio'd, or quietly leave. What sounds like "everyone agrees" is the chamber filtering, not the world.
Filter bubble vs echo chamber
A filter bubble is what the algorithm shows you. An echo chamber is what your community amplifies. Both reinforce each other.
Why "echo"
The same idea bounces back, slightly louder each time. People mistake the volume for evidence, "everyone thinks this", when really the same people are speaking.
Tell-tale
When was the last time you saw a thoughtful disagreement on this topic, in this space?

Why This Matters · Preview of Module 2
27 / 44

Why this matters.

Coordinated influence campaigns and propaganda thrive in feeds that are optimised for engagement. Recognising the mechanism is the first step in recognising the manipulation.
The compound effect
Algorithm + filter bubble + echo chamber + emotion-targeting content = an environment where coordinated deception is structurally favoured over careful reporting.
Worth holding in mind
Most of what reaches you is not malicious. But the few coordinated pushes that are malicious are extraordinarily well-suited to this terrain.
Coming up · Module 2
Reading critically & investigative thinking.
In Day 2 we'll go past "spotting" misleading content into reading it apart, bias, persuasion tactics, manipulation patterns, and the cognitive habits that make you harder to fool.

Section Four
28 / 44
04

Your rights
online.

You are not a passive user. You have rights, you have habits that protect them, and a few small changes this week will do more than any setting screen ever has.
Slides in this section
28 → 32
A Framing Question
29 / 44
Not a list of rules

What is digital citizenship?

Question to sit with
What do you want the online spaces you use to feel like, and what part do you play in shaping that?
Digital citizenship isn't a code of conduct. It's the recognition that your behaviour online makes those spaces better or worse for everyone around you.
Citizens, not users
"User" frames you as someone the platform serves. "Citizen" reminds you the platform is partly a public space you co-create.
Rights + responsibilities
You have rights worth defending, and your behaviour either respects or violates other people's.
Today's focus
The rights side: what you're owed, how to spot when a platform isn't honouring it, and what to do about it.
Four Core Rights
30 / 44

Your digital rights.

Not exhaustive. The four to know first.
RIGHT · 01
Privacy & protection of personal data.
What you share, who can see it, and what a platform can do with it should be your choice, not a default you missed.
Holds whether you're 13 or 73.
RIGHT · 02
Access to information & freedom of expression.
You can read, share and speak, within limits that protect others, without arbitrary suppression of legitimate speech.
Comes with responsibilities.
RIGHT · 03
Safety from harassment.
Threats, doxxing, targeted abuse, you have the right to use a platform without being subjected to these, and a way to report it.
Patchy in practice. Worth pushing on.
RIGHT · 04
The right to be forgotten.
In many jurisdictions you can request that data about you be deleted, and that old material no longer follow you indefinitely.
Best protected where data laws are strong.
A right is only as live as your awareness of it. Knowing it exists is the first half of using it.
Side-by-Side · Same Right
31 / 44

Respected vs violated.

For each right, what does it look like when a platform honours it, and when it doesn't? Noticing the difference is the first step.
RIGHT · 01 · PRIVACY
Privacy & data protection.
Respected
Clear, plain-language settings. Defaults that protect you. A real path to download or delete your data.
Violated
Defaults to "share publicly". Settings buried. Data sold without meaningful consent.
RIGHT · 02 · EXPRESSION
Freedom of expression & access to information.
Respected
Published rules, transparent enforcement, real appeal for take-downs, no arbitrary throttling.
Violated
Opaque "shadow-bans". No reasons given. Different rules for different accounts. No appeal.
RIGHT · 03 · SAFETY
Safety from harassment.
Respected
Working report flows, fast review of serious threats, blocking that actually blocks, support for targets.
Violated
"No violation found." Threats left up. Targets told to leave. Pile-ons monetised via engagement.
RIGHT · 04 · TO BE FORGOTTEN
Right to be forgotten.
Respected
Honoured deletion requests for legitimate cases. Old material removable. Backups handled too.
Violated
"Deleted" content still searchable. No mechanism for legitimate erasure. Old data resurfaced for ads.
Interactive · Tap to check off
32 / 44
Habits that protect you

Digital hygiene basics.

0 / 5 reviewed
Strong passwords + a password manager.
One per site. Long. Not reused. Let a manager remember them so you don't have to.
Two-factor authentication on every important account.
Email, bank, main social. Authenticator app preferred over SMS where offered.
Recognise & resist phishing.
Urgency + a link + a request for credentials = stop and verify out-of-band.
Review privacy settings on the platforms you actually use.
Once a year. 10 minutes per app. Pay attention to defaults.
Know what to do if an account is compromised.
Change password from a clean device · revoke sessions · enable 2FA if not already · check connected apps · alert anyone the account messaged.
Take-Home Preview
33 / 44
Programme Aim · 03

The easiest thing to pass on.

Of everything in this whole programme, digital hygiene habits are the simplest to share with friends and family this week. No vocabulary, no platforms-discussion, just five small actions that protect them now.
TAKE-HOME · CHECKLIST
For someone you love
Five habits. One conversation. This week.
  1. Strong, unique passwords, set up a password manager together.
  2. Turn on 2-factor authentication on email + main social.
  3. Show them what a phishing message looks like.
  4. Walk through privacy settings on one app they use daily.
  5. Agree on what they'll do if an account is hijacked, before it happens.
COPY THESE FIVE DOWN BEFORE YOU LEAVE
Why this
Most people in your life will never sit through a media-literacy workshop. They will sit through a ten-minute conversation with you.
A small ask
Before Day 2, have this conversation with one person. Any of the five. Just one.

Exercise · How It Works
35 / 44
Small groups · 5 minutes

How it works.

Activity Timer 05:00
The format
  1. Read three news articles, side by side.
  2. Two are real. One is fabricated.
  3. In groups of three or four, decide which is the fake.
  4. Crucially: note why, what tipped you off, or what raised doubt.
  5. Each group reports back. We'll do the reveal together.
Useful lenses while reading
Source, what's the outlet? Have you heard of it? Is the URL exactly right?
Byline & date, named reporter? Recent date? Specific or vague location?
Tone, does the language sound like reporting, or like persuasion?
Detail, specifics that could be checked, or claims that can't be?

The Reveal
38 / 44
Article B is the fake.

What gave it away.

Same article, annotated. Six signals, all visible on the page, before any external fact-checking.
FAKE
GLOBAL HEALTH BULLETIN
International · 3 days ago
Internal WHO memo confirms vaccine effectiveness against new variant "far lower than publicly stated", sources say
A document said to be circulating among senior staff at the agency suggests officials have been aware for weeks that a new strain reduces vaccine response by up to 71%, but have chosen not to make the finding public.
The memo has not been authenticated and was not provided in full. It was described to this outlet by "a person familiar with its contents". The 71% figure does not appear in any of the three peer-reviewed studies on the variant published this year. Shared 38,000 times in 18 hours…
By staff · globalhealthbulletin.co
Six signals
01
Lookalike outlet. "Global Health Bulletin" sounds authoritative, but it's not WHO, CIDRAP, or any recognised public-health body. Mimics legitimacy.
02
Suspicious domain. ".co" instead of an established health-body domain (who.int, cdc.gov). Common with cloned or look-alike health sites.
03
Generic byline. "By staff", no named health correspondent, no editor, nobody to hold accountable for the claim.
04
Sourcing two steps removed. A memo "said to be circulating", "described to this outlet by a person familiar". The document has "not been authenticated and was not provided in full". Nothing checkable.
05
A precise number with no method. "71%" sounds rigorous, but no study, sample size, methodology, or DOI is cited. Numbers without sources do persuasion, not science.
06
The article quietly disproves itself. Admits the figure "does not appear in any of the three peer-reviewed studies". Cites virality ("38,000 shares in 18 hours") in place of evidence.
Your Starting Toolkit
39 / 44

What you were already noticing.

The reasons each group gave back. Named, written down, this is your starting toolkit for Modules 2 and 3.
CUE 01
"The headline was screaming."
All-caps, exclamatory, emotionally extreme. Real reporting rarely shouts.
CUE 02
"I didn't recognise the outlet."
Or the name was almost right, but a letter off.
CUE 03
"There was no real name on it."
"Staff Writer", "Editorial Team", nobody to call.
CUE 04
"Nothing was actually checkable."
No names, no document, no date, no department.
CUE 05

Outrage, fear, urgency, pre-packaged in the deck.
CUE 06
"The URL looked off."
Unusual TLD, hyphens, suffixes like "-news" or "-today".
CUE 07
"It contradicted itself."
The body undid the headline's claim, quietly.
CUE 08
"It just felt off."
Trust the gut. Then check why.

Practical · The Moment You Spot It
40 / 44
When you see it

What you can do, today.

Three actions. Each is something you can do the moment you spot something misleading. None require expertise.
01
Report it where you found it.
The pattern is the same on every platform. Open the post's menu, choose Report, then pick the most specific category, "false information", "scam", "impersonation", not just "I don't like this".
Where to find Report
X / Twittertap ··· on the post › Report post Instagramtap ··· on the post › Report TikTokpress and hold the video › Report Facebooktap ··· on the post › Find support or report WhatsApppress and hold the message › Report
02
Don't share it on, even to dunk on it.
The algorithm doesn't distinguish between agreement and mockery. A reshare with "lol look at this nonsense" still counts as engagement, still gets amplified.
If you want to comment: screenshot, don't quote-share. The reach belongs to you, not the original post.
03
Talk to the person who shared it.
Where it feels safe to. In private, not in the comments. Lead with curiosity ("Where did this come from?"), not correction.
Most people who share misinformation aren't bad, they're rushed. A quiet "hey" matters more than a public correction.
